mainTopic: Dividing short Torah readings (דולג and פוסק), and how many people read on a תענית צבור
overview: On ראש חודש four people read from the תורה, but the paragraphs are short, and every way of dividing them seems to break a three-verse rule. רבא answers from a similar case, the מעמדות reading of בראשית, where five verses were shared by two readers. In that case רב said the second reader repeats a verse (דולג), and שמואל said a verse is split (פוסק). The גמרא explains the reasons for each view and shows that these methods are used only when there is no other option. רבי יהושע בן לוי rules that a reader may not begin a paragraph with fewer than three verses or stop with fewer than three left, and רב יוסף rules that the middle reader repeats a verse. The גמרא then asks how many people read on a תענית צבור. Proofs from the wording of the משנה cancel out. A story about רב reading on a fast day in בבל is debated back and forth, and the discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: No good way to divide the last paragraphs
steps.stepSummary: The questioner shows that reading two verses from וביום השבת and three from ובראשי חדשיכם leaves only two verses, which is not enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: One may not begin a new paragraph and read fewer than three verses from it. And if you say the reader should read the two verses of this paragraph and three verses of that one, only two verses are left!
steps.whatsHappening: The questioner finishes his problem. He tries one more way to divide the ראש חודש reading and shows that it also fails.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first rule says that if a reader starts a new paragraph, he must read at least three of its verses. So a reader could take the two verses of וביום השבת plus three verses of ובראשי חדשיכם. But that leaves only two verses of the last paragraph. That is not enough for the fourth reader, and it also means stopping with fewer than three verses left in a paragraph.

keyTerms.meaning: A paragraph or section of the תורה
Fewer than three verses
Let him read
From this one / from that one
Are left over, remain

steps.confusionAlert: "This" (מהא) means the two-verse paragraph וביום השבת. "That" (מהך) means the five-verse paragraph ובראשי חדשיכם. The problem is the two verses left at the end, not the two verses of וביום השבת.

phrases.english: One may not begin a paragraph
and read fewer than three verses from it.
phrases.notes: If you start a new paragraph, you must read at least three of its verses.

phrases.english: Let him read two verses from this paragraph
phrases.notes: This is the paragraph וביום השבת, which has only two verses.

phrases.english: and three from that paragraph,
phrases.notes: This is the paragraph ובראשי חדשיכם, which has five verses.

phrases.english: then only two are left!
phrases.notes: Not enough for the next reader, and you may not stop with fewer than three verses left in a paragraph.

steps.triggerLanguage: לִיקְרֵי תְּרֵי מֵהָא וּתְלָתָא מֵהָךְ, פָּשׁוּ לְהוּ תְּרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the question that began on the previous amud about how to divide the ראש חודש reading.
steps.kashyaTarget: Every possible way of dividing the ראש חודש reading among four readers
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Read two verses plus three, and two verses remain. That breaks the rule of not leaving fewer than three verses in a paragraph, and the last reader cannot get three verses.

steps.title: רבא brings a similar case from the מעמדות reading
steps.stepSummary: רבא says he never heard an answer to this exact case, but he heard one for a similar case: בראשית was read by two people and יהי רקיע by one.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: This I have not heard, but I have heard something similar. As we learned in a משנה: On the first day of the week they read "בראשית" and "יהי רקיע". And a ברייתא taught about it: "בראשית" was read by two people, and "יהי רקיע" by one.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא starts his answer by pointing to a similar case. This step sets up the case that the next steps will use to solve the problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The אנשי מעמד read the creation story each day of the week. On Sunday the paragraph בראשית has only five verses, yet two people read it. That is the same kind of problem: a short paragraph that must be shared while each reader gets three verses.

keyTerms.meaning: This I have not heard (from my teachers)
Something similar to it
As we learned in a משנה
And a ברייתא taught about it
By two readers / by one reader

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows a common way the גמרא answers: when there is no direct tradition, it reasons from a parallel case that does have one.

phrases.english: He said to him: This I have not heard,
but something similar to it I have heard,
as we learned in a mishna: On the first day (Sunday) —
phrases.notes: This משנה is in תענית 26a, and it's about what the אנשי מעמד read.

phrases.english: they read "In the beginning" and "Let there be a firmament,"
phrases.notes: בראשית has 5 verses; יהי רקיע has 3 verses

phrases.english: and it was taught about it:
"In the beginning" is read by two people,
"Let there be a firmament" by one.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ: זוֹ לֹא שָׁמַעְתִּי, כַּיּוֹצֵא בָּהּ שָׁמַעְתִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the problem in step 1 by bringing in a similar case.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: There is no direct tradition, but the similar case of בראשית being read by two people will show how to solve it.
steps.raayaSupportSource: משנה in תענית and the ברייתא on it about the מעמדות reading

steps.title: How can two people share five verses?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא there asked: יהי רקיע by one reader is fine, but how can two people read בראשית when it has only five verses?
steps.simpleTranslation: And we discussed it: It makes sense that "יהי רקיע" is read by one person, since it has three verses. But how can "בראשית" be read by two? It has only five verses, and it was taught: One who reads from the תורה may not read fewer than three verses!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא repeats the difficulty that the earlier discussion raised about the בראשית case. It is the same problem as in step 1.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Three verses for one reader works perfectly. But two readers who each need three verses would need six, and בראשית has only five. So the earlier גמרא had to deal with the very same shortage.

keyTerms.meaning: And we discussed it / raised a difficulty about it
It makes sense that... (sets up a contrast with אלא)
But... (introduces the difficult part)
And it was taught (introduces a תנאי source)

phrases.english: And we discussed it:
It makes sense that "Let there be a firmament" is read by one,
since it has three verses,
but how can "In the beginning" be read by two?
It has only five verses,
and it was taught: One who reads from the Torah
may not read fewer than three verses!
phrases.notes: Two readers × three verses = six, but there are only five.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Raises a difficulty against the ברייתא brought in step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that בראשית is read by two people
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Five verses cannot give two readers three verses each, but the rule requires at least three verses for every reader.

steps.title: רב repeats a verse, שמואל splits a verse
steps.stepSummary: רב says the second reader repeats a verse. שמואל says the third verse is split in half.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it was said about it: רב said: He repeats a verse. And שמואל said: He splits a verse.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים answer how five verses can be shared by two readers. This is the tradition רבא will use for the ראש חודש problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב: the first reader reads verses 1-3, and the second reader goes back and reads verses 3-5. Verse 3 is read twice, so each reader gets three verses. שמואל: verse 3 is cut in half, the first reader stops in the middle of it, and the second reader starts from that point, so each half counts as a verse.

keyTerms.meaning: And it was said about it (by the אמוראים)
Repeats (lit. "jumps" back): the next reader re-reads a verse the previous reader already read
Splits: divides one verse into two halves

steps.whatToRemember: When there are not enough verses to give each reader three, רב says דולג (repeat a verse) and שמואל says פוסק (split a verse). רבא brings this מחלוקת as the model for dividing the short ראש חודש paragraphs.
steps.confusionAlert: Here דולג does not mean skipping ahead past verses. It means jumping back and repeating a verse that was already read.
steps.whyThisMatters: This מחלוקת is the basis for how short קריאות התורה, like the one on ראש חודש, are divided in practice.

phrases.english: And it was stated about it:
Rav said: He repeats.
phrases.notes: The second reader re-reads the last verse of the first reader.

phrases.english: And Shmuel said: He splits.
phrases.notes: The middle verse is divided, and each half counts as a verse.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיתְּמַר עֲלַהּ, רַב אָמַר: דּוֹלֵג. וּשְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר: פּוֹסֵק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the difficulty in step 3, and gives the model for the problem in step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical method that makes up for missing verses
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Five verses cannot be shared by two readers.
steps.terutzMaskana: It can be done, either by repeating a verse (רב) or by splitting a verse (שמואל).

steps.title: Why didn't רב say to split the verse?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רב chose repeating a פסוק (דולג) instead of splitting one (פוסק).
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said the second reader repeats a verse. What is his reason for not saying that the verse is split?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a question about רב's view. It wants to know why רב rejected שמואל's simpler idea of splitting the middle פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Splitting the third פסוק looks like an easy fix, since each reader would get two and a half פסוקים. So רב must have a reason for avoiding it. The answer comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Repeats or skips back. The second reader starts again from the last פסוק the first reader read.
Splits. One פסוק is divided in half.
What is the reason?

phrases.english: Rav said: he repeats [a verse],
phrases.notes: This quotes רב's view from the previous step.

phrases.english: what is the reason he did not say: he splits [the verse]?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind רב's answer from step 4.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why רב preferred repeating a פסוק over splitting one.

steps.title: רב holds a verse may not be split
steps.stepSummary: רב holds that any פסוק that משה did not divide, we may not divide.
steps.simpleTranslation: He holds: any verse that משה did not divide, we may not divide.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רב believes the divisions between פסוקים go back to משה, so we cannot cut a פסוק in the middle.
steps.deeperAnalysis: To רב, the boundaries of a פסוק are fixed, so splitting one is forbidden. Repeating a whole פסוק breaks no boundary, so רב picks that option. The next step asks how שמואל can allow splitting.

keyTerms.meaning: He holds (his opinion is)
A verse (פסוק)
משה divided it, meaning the פסוק boundaries go back to משה.

steps.whyThisMatters: This rule, that a פסוק not divided by משה may not be divided, becomes the basis for the challenge against שמואל in the next step.

phrases.english: He holds: any verse
that Moshe did not divide,
we may not divide it.

steps.triggerLanguage: קָסָבַר: כֹּל פְּסוּקָא דְּלָא פַּסְקֵיהּ מֹשֶׁה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב holds that a פסוק not divided by משה may not be divided, so he must use repeating instead.

steps.title: Challenge to שמואל: splitting was allowed only for children
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges שמואל from רבי חנניא קרא, whose teacher allowed splitting פסוקים only for schoolchildren.
steps.simpleTranslation: And does שמואל say we may divide a verse? But רבי חנניא קרא said: I had great difficulty with רבי חנינא הגדול, and he allowed me to divide verses only for schoolchildren, since they need it in order to learn.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks שמואל's view. A known story shows that splitting a פסוק was normally forbidden and was allowed only for young students.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חנניא קרא was a Bible teacher who wanted to split long פסוקים. His teacher רבי חנינא הגדול refused except for children, who cannot learn a long פסוק all at once. So how can שמואל allow splitting for a regular קריאת התורה?

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't [so-and-so] say? A formula that introduces a challenge.
Bible expert (a title for רבי חנניא)
Schoolchildren learning תורה
They are there in order to learn.

phrases.english: And does Shmuel say we may divide it?
But didn't Rabbi Chananya the Bible expert say:
I had great distress
with Rabbi Chanina the Great,
and he did not permit me to divide [verses]
except for schoolchildren,
since they are there to be taught.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּשְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר פָּסְקִינַן לֵיהּ? וְהָא אָמַר רַבִּי חֲנַנְיָא קָרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the ban on splitting from step 6, backed by a story, to challenge שמואל's answer in step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's view that the middle פסוק is split (פוסק).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי חנינא הגדול allowed splitting only for schoolchildren. That implies splitting is normally forbidden, so it should be forbidden in קריאת התורה too.

steps.title: Both cases have no other option
steps.stepSummary: Splitting was allowed for children because there was no other way. Here too there is no other way, so splitting is allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, what is the reason? Because it is not possible otherwise. Here too, it is not possible otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends שמואל. It says the children's case was allowed because there was no choice, and our case is also one with no choice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ban on splitting is not absolute. It gives way when there is no other option. Children cannot learn a long פסוק without breaking it up, and two readers cannot each read three פסוקים out of five without splitting one, so שמואל allows it.

keyTerms.meaning: There (in the other case)
Here too
It is not possible (there is no other option).

phrases.english: There, what is the reason?
Because it is not possible [otherwise];
here too, it is not possible [otherwise].

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם טַעְמָא מַאי — מִשּׁוּם דְּלָא אֶפְשָׁר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the reason behind the source (the permission was based on necessity, not on the fact that they were children).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Splitting a פסוק is allowed only for schoolchildren.
steps.terutzMaskana: Splitting is allowed whenever there is no other option, and dividing five פסוקים between two readers is such a case.

steps.title: Why didn't שמואל say to repeat a verse?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why שמואל did not accept רב's option of repeating a פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: And שמואל said the verse is split. What is his reason for not saying that the second reader repeats a verse?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the matching question for שמואל. Repeating a whole פסוק seems to avoid any splitting, so why not do that?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since step 8 called splitting a last resort, repeating would seem better. So שמואל must see a problem with repeating. The answer comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: And שמואל said (introduces his view for analysis)

phrases.english: And Shmuel said: he splits [the verse],
what is the reason he did not say: he repeats [a verse]?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Mirrors step 5. Having asked why רב rejects splitting, the גמרא now asks why שמואל rejects repeating.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why שמואל preferred splitting over repeating.

steps.title: Repeating could mislead people entering and leaving
steps.stepSummary: שמואל rejects repeating because of a גזירה: people who walk in or out of the בית כנסת in the middle could be misled.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a decree because of those who come in and because of those who go out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that שמואל avoids repeating because of a rabbinic decree (גזירה) that protects people who walk in or out during the reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Suppose the second reader repeats פסוק 3 and reads 3, 4, 5. Someone who walks in late hears three פסוקים and assumes, since the section has only five, that the first reader read just two. Someone who leaves after the first reading (1, 2, 3) assumes the second reader will read only two. Either way, people would wrongly think a reading of two פסוקים is allowed, so שמואל prefers splitting.

keyTerms.meaning: A rabbinic decree made to prevent a mistake
Those who enter (the בית כנסת)
Those who leave

steps.whatToRemember: רב says repeat (דולג) because a פסוק not divided by משה may not be split. שמואל says split (פוסק) because there is no other option, and repeating would mislead people who come in or leave. Both agree each reader must read at least three פסוקים.
steps.confusionAlert: The worry is not about the people inside the room the whole time. They know a פסוק was repeated. The worry is only about people who hear just one of the two readings and then wrongly conclude that the other reading was only two פסוקים.

phrases.english: A decree because of those who enter
and because of those who leave.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 9.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Repeating a פסוק could lead people who come in or go out to think a reading of only two פסוקים is valid, so שמואל requires splitting instead.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Each view rests on its own concern. רב's concern is not breaking a פסוק boundary. שמואל's concern is not misleading people who hear only part of the reading.

steps.title: Quoting a ברייתא about dividing short paragraphs
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins a challenge by quoting a ברייתא. The ברייתא says a 6-verse paragraph may be split between two readers, but a 5-verse paragraph needs one reader. If the first reads 3 of the 5, the second reads the last 2 plus verses from the next paragraph. The תנא קמא says 1 verse is enough; the יש אומרים require 3.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: A paragraph of six verses may be read by two people, and a paragraph of five verses by one person. If the first person read three, the second reads two from this paragraph and one from the next paragraph. Some say: three from the next paragraph, because one may not begin a paragraph and read fewer than three verses.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is quoting a ברייתא to set up a challenge against רב and שמואל. The actual attack comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each reader must read at least three פסוקים. So six verses can be split 3 and 3, but five verses cannot be split fairly. The ברייתא's fix is to continue into the next paragraph. It never mentions repeating a verse or splitting a verse.

keyTerms.meaning: They challenged (introduces a source that seems to contradict an opinion)
A paragraph or section of the תורה
By a single reader
Some say (a second opinion in the ברייתא)
We do not begin

steps.confusionAlert: פרשה here means a short paragraph in the ספר תורה, not the weekly פרשת השבוע.

phrases.english: They challenged: a paragraph of six verses
is read by two people,
phrases.notes: Three verses for each reader.

phrases.english: and one of five verses by a single reader.
phrases.notes: Five verses cannot give two readers three each.

phrases.english: If the first read three,
phrases.notes: From the five-verse paragraph.

phrases.english: the second reads two from this paragraph
phrases.notes: The two verses that are left.

phrases.english: and one from another paragraph.
phrases.notes: This brings him to three verses in total.

phrases.english: And some say: three,
phrases.notes: Three verses from the next paragraph.

phrases.english: because one may not begin a paragraph
with fewer than three verses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings an outside source against both רב's repeating and שמואל's splitting.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Setup only: the ברייתא handles a short paragraph without repeating or splitting a פסוק. The attack itself comes in step 12.

steps.title: Why didn't the ברייתא suggest repeating or splitting?
steps.stepSummary: If רב and שמואל are right, the ברייתא should have told the second reader to repeat a verse (רב) or split a verse (שמואל).
steps.simpleTranslation: And if it is so, according to the one who says he repeats, let him repeat; and according to the one who says he splits, let him split!
steps.whatsHappening: This is the punchline of the challenge. If repeating or splitting were valid, the ברייתא should have used one of them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Leaving it out suggests these options are not allowed. One question attacks both אמוראים, each according to his own method.

keyTerms.meaning: And if it is so (if your view were correct)
Skips back, meaning he repeats a verse already read (רב)
Splits a verse in the middle (שמואל)

phrases.english: And if it is so,
phrases.notes: If repeating or splitting were allowed.

phrases.english: according to the one who says he repeats, let him repeat,
phrases.notes: Aimed at רב.

phrases.english: and according to the one who says he splits, let him split!
phrases.notes: Aimed at שמואל.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם אִיתָא, לְמַאן דְּאָמַר דּוֹלֵג — נִדְלוֹג
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the quoted ברייתא into a direct challenge.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא does not mention their solutions, which implies the solutions are not valid.

steps.title: There, another option was available
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא's case is different because the reader can simply continue into the next paragraph. On ראש חודש that option does not exist.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is different there, because it is possible to do it this way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב and שמואל. The ברייתא had an easier solution, so it did not need theirs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברייתא, the next paragraph can be added to the reading. On ראש חודש, the next paragraph is about a different topic and cannot be read. So repeating or splitting is used only when there is no other way.

keyTerms.meaning: It is different there
It is possible this way

steps.whyThisMatters: This repeats the rule from step 8: repeating or splitting a פסוק is a last resort, used only when nothing else works.

phrases.english: It is different there,
phrases.notes: In the ברייתא's case.

phrases.english: because it is possible this way.
phrases.notes: By reading on into the next paragraph.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (אפשר versus אי אפשר)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא's silence shows that repeating or splitting is never allowed.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא skipped those options only because it had a simpler one. On ראש חודש there is none, so רב and שמואל's solutions stand.

steps.title: The הלכה follows the יש אומרים
steps.stepSummary: רבי תנחום, quoting רבי יהושע בן לוי, rules like the יש אומרים: the second reader must read three verses from the new paragraph.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי תנחום said in the name of רבי יהושע בן לוי: The הלכה follows the יש אומרים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives a practical ruling on the disagreement inside the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא had two views: read one verse from the next paragraph, or read three. The ruling is three, because you may not begin a paragraph with fewer than three פסוקים.

keyTerms.meaning: The practical law follows...
A leading אמורא of ארץ ישראל

phrases.english: Rabbi Tanchum said
that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
the law follows the "some say" opinion,
phrases.notes: At least three verses from the new paragraph.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי תַּנְחוּם אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי: הֲלָכָה כְּיֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the ברייתא and decides between its two views.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Do not begin a paragraph with fewer than three פסוקים.

steps.title: Don't leave fewer than three verses at the end
steps.stepSummary: The same chain of teachers adds a matching rule: just as you may not start a paragraph with fewer than three verses, you may not stop a reading leaving fewer than three verses in the paragraph.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי תנחום said in the name of רבי יהושע בן לוי: Just as one may not begin a paragraph with fewer than three verses, so too one may not leave fewer than three verses in a paragraph.
steps.whatsHappening: A second ruling is added that mirrors the first, this time about where a reader may stop.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first rule is about where a reading starts. This rule is about where it ends. A reader may not stop with only one or two verses left in the paragraph.

keyTerms.meaning: Just as... so too
Leave over

steps.whatToRemember: Three-verse rules: each reader reads at least three פסוקים, you may not begin a paragraph with fewer than three, and you may not stop leaving fewer than three in the paragraph. Repeating (רב) or splitting (שמואל) a פסוק is used only when there is no other way.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Tanchum said
that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
Just as one may not begin a paragraph
with fewer than three verses,
so too one may not leave over in a paragraph
phrases.notes: When a reader finishes his portion.

phrases.english: fewer than three verses.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי תַּנְחוּם אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי: כְּשֵׁם שֶׁאֵין מַתְחִילִין בַּפָּרָשָׁה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a matching rule for the end of a paragraph.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A reader may not stop leaving fewer than three פסוקים in the paragraph.

steps.title: Why say the rule about leaving verses? It seems obvious
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי יהושע בן לוי's second rule. If the יש אומרים are strict about starting a paragraph, where the תנא קמא is lenient, they must surely be strict about leaving verses, where even the תנא קמא is strict.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is obvious! Think about it. At the start of a paragraph, the תנא קמא is lenient, and still the יש אומרים are strict. At the end of a paragraph (leaving verses), even the תנא קמא is strict. So of course the יש אומרים are strict there too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רבי יהושע בן לוי needed to teach the rule about not leaving fewer than three verses. It seems we could have figured it out on our own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a קל וחומר. The יש אומרים are stricter than the תנא קמא even where the תנא קמא is lenient, which is starting a paragraph. So where the תנא קמא himself is already strict, which is leaving verses at the end, the יש אומרים must certainly be strict. The second ruling (Step 15) therefore looks unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious. Used to challenge a statement as unnecessary.
The beginning of a paragraph
Leaving over verses at the end of a paragraph
All the more so (a קל וחומר argument)

phrases.english: This is obvious!
Now, if at the beginning of a paragraph,
where the first tanna is lenient,
phrases.notes: He requires only one verse from the new paragraph.

phrases.english: the 'some say' are stringent,
phrases.notes: They require three verses.

phrases.english: then regarding leaving verses, where the first tanna is stringent,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא כׇּל שֶׁכֵּן דְּמַחְמְירִי יֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים?!
phrases.english: is it not all the more so that the 'some say' are stringent?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for the ruling in Step 15
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהושע בן לוי's ruling that one may not leave fewer than three verses in a paragraph
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A קל וחומר from the יש אומרים being strict about starting a paragraph makes the ruling about leaving verses obvious and unnecessary.

steps.title: We might have thought people rarely walk out
steps.stepSummary: The rule was needed. Without it, we might have said that people often come in late but rarely leave in the middle, so the יש אומרים would not worry about leaving verses.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have thought: people often come in during the reading, but people rarely leave in the middle, walking out on a ספר תורה. So the rule teaches us that the יש אומרים worry about this too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by showing that the ruling teaches something new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The concern behind 'leaving' is that someone walks out right after a reading and thinks the next reader will read fewer than three verses. Someone could argue that walking out during קריאת התורה is rare, so there is no need to worry. רבי יהושע בן לוי teaches that the יש אומרים do worry about it, so the קל וחומר alone would not have been enough.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said. Introduces a mistaken assumption.
People who enter the בית כנסת during the reading
People who leave the בית כנסת during the reading
It teaches us (that the assumption is wrong)

phrases.english: You might have said:
people entering is common,
people leaving is not common,
meaning they would abandon a Torah scroll and walk out,
so it teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא challenge
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the ruling is necessary by refuting a possible assumption (מהו דתימא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Walking out during the reading is rare, so the יש אומרים would not forbid leaving fewer than three verses.
steps.terutzMaskana: The יש אומרים also worry about people who leave, so one may not leave fewer than three verses.

steps.title: Why does the תנא קמא worry only about people leaving?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks about the תנא קמא. He forbids leaving fewer than three verses because of people who leave. So why doesn't he also forbid starting with fewer than three verses because of people who come in?
steps.simpleTranslation: And the תנא קמא: why is leaving verses different? He forbids it because of people who leave. Then for starting a paragraph, he should also make a גזירה because of people who come in!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now questions whether the תנא קמא is consistent. He seems to worry about one group of people but not the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא is strict about leaving fewer than three verses, out of concern for people walking out. By the same logic, someone coming in late might see a reader read only one verse of a new paragraph and think he read just one verse. Since the תנא קמא allows one verse at the start, the גמרא asks why he does not worry about latecomers.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difference? Asks why two cases are treated differently.
A rabbinic decree made to prevent a mistake
Starting a new paragraph

phrases.english: And according to the first tanna, what is different
about leaving verses, which is not allowed because of those who leave?
For starting a paragraph, too,
there should be a decree because of those who enter!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the יש אומרים to a consistency challenge against the תנא קמא
steps.kashyaTarget: The תנא קמא's distinction between starting a paragraph (one verse is enough) and leaving verses (three are needed)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the concern about people leaving makes him strict at the end, the parallel concern about people entering should make him strict at the start.

steps.title: A latecomer asks what he missed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that someone who comes in late asks what was read. He will be told the reader started earlier, so there is no mistake to worry about.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: whoever comes in asks questions.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the תנא קמא is not worried about people who come in late.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person who walks in during the reading naturally asks what is going on. He will learn that the reader started in the earlier paragraph, so he will not think the reader read too few verses. A person who walks out does not ask anything afterward, so his mistake is never corrected. That is why the תנא קמא worries only about him.

keyTerms.meaning: They say. Introduces an answer.
Enters
Asks

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the two concerns are equal. The difference is not how common each case is. The person entering will ask and be corrected, but the person leaving will not.

phrases.english: They say: one who enters
definitely asks.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the consistency challenge against the תנא קמא
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes the two cases on practical grounds
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The latecomer's possible mistake should be treated like the mistake of someone who walks out.
steps.terutzMaskana: The latecomer asks and is corrected. The person who walks out is not, so only leaving verses needs a גזירה.

steps.title: רבה בריה דרבא asks רב יוסף for the הלכה
steps.stepSummary: רבה בריה דרבא sends a question to רב יוסף: what is the final הלכה about dividing a short paragraph between readers?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה, the son of רבא, sent to רב יוסף: What is the הלכה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up the practical ruling. A question is sent asking for the final הלכה, and the answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the גמרא brought two approaches for a short paragraph like the one on ראש חודש. רב says the reader repeats a verse, and שמואל says he splits a verse. This question asks which approach we actually follow.

keyTerms.meaning: He sent to him (a written or messenger question)
What is the הלכה?

phrases.english: Rabba, son of Rava, sent
to Rav Yosef:
What is the halakha?

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁלַח לֵיהּ רַבָּה בְּרֵיהּ דְּרָבָא לְרַב יוֹסֵף: הִלְכְתָא מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns from the side discussion to the main dispute between רב and שמואל
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether we follow רב (repeat a verse) or שמואל (split a verse) when dividing a short paragraph

steps.title: The הלכה: repeat a verse, and the middle reader does it
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף rules like רב: the reader repeats a verse. It is the middle reader who repeats it, so that no one ends leaving fewer than three verses in the paragraph.
steps.simpleTranslation: He sent back to him: The הלכה is that one repeats a verse, and it is the middle reader who repeats.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף gives the final practical ruling, following רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The הלכה follows רב, so a verse is repeated rather than split. רב יוסף adds that the middle reader is the one who repeats. This fits the rule from Step 15 that a reader may not stop leaving fewer than three verses in the paragraph.

keyTerms.meaning: Repeats (literally 'skips back') a verse the previous reader already read
The middle reader

steps.whatToRemember: The rule that you may not leave fewer than three verses in a paragraph is needed even for the יש אומרים, because we might have thought people rarely walk out. The תנא קמא worries only about people leaving, because a latecomer asks what he missed. The final הלכה: when a paragraph is too short, a verse is repeated (like רב), and the middle reader is the one who repeats it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the practical ruling for dividing the ראש חודש קריאה among the readers.

phrases.english: He sent back to him:
The halakha is: one repeats a verse,
phrases.notes: This follows רב, not שמואל.

phrases.english: and it is the middle reader who repeats.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁלַח לֵיהּ, הִלְכְתָא: דּוֹלֵג, וְאֶמְצָעִי דּוֹלְגָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in Step 20
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The הלכה follows רב: a verse is repeated, and the middle reader is the one who repeats it.

steps.title: How many people read on a public fast?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's rule about days with a מוסף. It then asks whether a תענית צבור gets three or four readers.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'This is the rule: any day that has a מוסף,' and so on. A question was asked: on a תענית צבור, how many people read? Maybe only ראש חודש and חול המועד get four, because they have a מוסף offering, and a fast day does not. Or maybe a fast day also gets four, because it has an added prayer.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question about our משנה: does a תענית צבור get three readers or four? It lays out two possible sides.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה ties four readers to having a מוסף. The question is what counts as a מוסף for this rule. If it means only an extra קרבן, a fast day gets three readers. If it also includes an extra prayer (the fast-day עננו), a fast day gets four.

keyTerms.meaning: This is the general rule
A question was asked among the scholars
A public fast day
The extra offering brought in the בית המקדש on special days
An extra prayer, meaning the added fast-day prayer עננו
Or perhaps (introduces the other side of a question)

steps.confusionAlert: On a fast day, 'extra prayer' does NOT mean a מוסף שמונה עשרה. It means the added prayer עננו that is inserted on fast days.

phrases.aramaic: זֶה הַכְּלָל, כֹּל שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ מוּסָף וְכוּ׳.
phrases.english: This is the rule: any day that has a Musaf, etc.
phrases.notes: Quoting the משנה

phrases.english: A question was asked: on a public fast, how many read?
Rosh Chodesh and the intermediate Festival days
which have an additional offering get four,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל הָכָא דְּלֵיכָּא קׇרְבַּן מוּסַף — לָא.
phrases.english: but here, where there is no additional offering, no.

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא: הָכָא נָמֵי אִיכָּא מוּסַף תְּפִלָּה.
phrases.english: Or perhaps here too there is an additional prayer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the topic of dividing short paragraphs and returns to the next line of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a תענית צבור get four readers like days with a מוסף, or only three?

steps.title: Proof from the משנה: only ראש חודש and חול המועד get four
steps.stepSummary: The משנה lists only ראש חודש and חול המועד as four-reader days. That seems to imply a fast day gets only three.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: the משנה says that on ראש חודש and חול המועד four people read. That implies that on a תענית צבור only three read!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to answer the question from the wording of the משנה itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה names ראש חודש and חול המועד as the days with four readers. If fast days also had four, the משנה should have listed them too. Leaving them out suggests fast days have three.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear (introduces a proof)
The intermediate days of a Festival (חול המועד)
This implies (introduces an inference from wording)

phrases.english: Come and hear: on Rosh Chodesh
and on Chol HaMoed, four people read,
which implies that on a public fast, three!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: בְּרָאשֵׁי חֳדָשִׁים וּבְחוּלּוֹ שֶׁל מוֹעֵד קוֹרִין אַרְבָּעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a proof for the first side of the question.
steps.raayaObject: A fast day gets three readers.
steps.raayaSupportSource: Inference from the wording of the משנה, which lists only ראש חודש and חול המועד as four-reader days.

steps.title: The first clause of the משנה implies the opposite
steps.stepSummary: The earlier line of the משנה lists only Monday, Thursday and שבת מנחה as three-reader days. That would imply a fast day gets four.
steps.simpleTranslation: Look at the first part of the משנה: on Monday, Thursday and שבת at מנחה, three people read. That implies that on a תענית צבור four read!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof. It shows that the same kind of reasoning, applied to an earlier line of the משנה, gives the opposite answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If leaving fast days off the four-reader list means they get three, then leaving them off the three-reader list should mean they get four. The two inferences cancel each other out.

keyTerms.meaning: Look at (say) the first clause
Monday and Thursday
The afternoon prayer

phrases.english: Say the first clause:

phrases.aramaic: בְּשֵׁנִי וּבַחֲמִישִׁי וּבַשַּׁבָּת בַּמִּנְחָה קוֹרִין שְׁלֹשָׁה:
phrases.english: On Monday, Thursday, and Shabbat at Minchah, three people read:
which implies that on a public fast, four!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of step 23 by showing an opposite inference.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects relying on the משנה's wording for this question.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Reasoning from what the משנה leaves out works in both directions, so it proves nothing.

steps.title: Nothing can be learned from the משנה
steps.stepSummary: Since the two inferences contradict each other, the משנה gives no answer about fast days.
steps.simpleTranslation: So we cannot learn anything about this from the משנה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes this first attempt. The question about fast days is still open.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה simply did not deal with fast days. That is why we cannot draw a conclusion from either of its lines.

keyTerms.meaning: Nothing can be learned from it

phrases.english: Rather, nothing can be learned from this.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Concludes the back-and-forth over the משנה's wording.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The משנה does not settle how many read on a תענית צבור.

steps.title: The story of רב reading on a fast day in בבל
steps.stepSummary: רב came to בבל on a fast day and read from the תורה. He made the opening ברכה but not the closing one. He also did not fall on his face for תחנון with everyone else.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: רב came to בבל on a תענית צבור. He stood up and read from the ספר תורה. When he started he made a ברכה, but when he finished he did not make a ברכה. Everyone fell on their faces for תחנון, but רב did not fall on his face.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a story as a second try at answering the question. This step only tells the story; the next step draws the proof from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key detail is that רב made no closing ברכה. Under the original rule of the משנה, only the first reader made the opening ברכה and only the last reader made the closing one. The next step uses that rule to work out how many people read. The part about not falling on his face is a side detail here and is not part of this proof.

keyTerms.meaning: Happened to come to a place
A Torah scroll
He opened with a ברכה
He finished without a ברכה
Falling on the face during תחנון

steps.confusionAlert: Today every person called up makes a ברכה before and after reading. Under the original rule of the משנה (הפותח והחותם מברך), only the first reader said the opening ברכה and only the last reader said the closing one. The proof in the next step assumes that original rule. Later the חכמים made a תקנה that every reader blesses (see step 32).

phrases.english: Come and hear: Rav happened to come to Babylonia
on a public fast; he stood and read from a Torah scroll.
He began with a blessing, he concluded without a blessing.
Everyone fell on their faces,
but Rav did not fall on his face.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: דְּרַב אִיקְּלַע לְבָבֶל בְּתַעֲנִית צִבּוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof from the משנה failed, brings a new source: a story.
steps.raayaObject: How many people read on a תענית צבור.
steps.raayaSupportSource: What רב did when he read from the Torah on a fast day in Bavel.

steps.title: רב was the third reader, so someone must have read after him
steps.stepSummary: רב read the ישראל portion, which is the third reading. Since he made no closing ברכה, it seems a fourth person read after him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now, רב read as a ישראל. So why did he finish without a ברכה? Isn't it because someone else was going to read after him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws the proof from the story. It argues that רב's missing closing ברכה shows there was a fourth reader on the fast day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב was not a כהן or a לוי, so he read third, as a ישראל. If only three people read, he would have been last and would have made the closing ברכה. Since he did not, someone else must have read after him, which means four readers on a fast day.

keyTerms.meaning: Now, since (sets up a logical argument)
A regular Jew who is not a כהן or לוי; he reads third
Is it not because...? (introduces a suggested reason)

steps.whyThisMatters: If this proof stands, it would decide the question: a תענית צבור has four readers, because an extra prayer counts like a מוסף.

phrases.english: Now, Rav read the Israelite's portion,
why did he conclude without a blessing?
Is it not because there needed to be
another person reading after him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how the story in step 26 proves that a fast day has four readers.
steps.raayaObject: A תענית צבור has four readers.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב read third (as a ישראל) and did not make the closing ברכה, so someone must have read after him.

steps.title: Maybe רב read the first portion, like רב הונא did
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected. רב may have read the first portion, the כהן's spot, and not the third.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. רב read the portion of the כהנים, just as רב הונא would read the portion of the כהנים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof from step 27. It says רב may not have read third at all. He may have read first, the spot usually given to a כהן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof needed רב to be the third reader. Only then would his missing closing ברכה show that a fourth person came after him. If רב read first, a missing closing ברכה is normal, because in those days only the last reader said the closing ברכה. So nothing is proven about a fourth reader. As support, the גמרא points out that רב הונא, the great leader of his generation, used to read first even though he was not a כהן.

keyTerms.meaning: In the portion of the כהנים, meaning the first reading
He read (from the תורה)
A great אמורא and leader of the תורה world in בבל

steps.confusionAlert: רב was not a כהן. The phrase 'he read בכהני' means he took the first slot, which is normally the כהן's slot, because he was the leading גדול of the generation.

phrases.english: No, Rav read in the priests' portion.
phrases.notes: He took the first reading, not the third.

phrases.english: For Rav Huna would read in the priests' portion.
phrases.notes: A precedent for a great leader reading first.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference of step 27 by changing which portion רב read.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof that a fourth person read on the fast day.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed רב read third. He may have read first, so the missing closing ברכה proves nothing.

steps.title: רב הונא was the top leader, but רב deferred to שמואל, who was a כהן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the comparison. רב הונא had no rival, but רב gave honor to שמואל, who was a כהן.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense that רב הונא read the כהנים' portion. Even רב אמי and רב אסי, the most important כהנים in ארץ ישראל, deferred to רב הונא. But רב? There was שמואל, who was a כהן, and רב placed him above himself!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the comparison between רב and רב הונא. It argues that רב was not the single unrivaled leader, so he would not have taken a כהן's place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A non-כהן may read first only if he is the undisputed leader, someone even the great כהנים bow to. רב הונא fit that description, since even the top כהנים deferred to him. רב, however, honored שמואל, a כהן, as greater than himself. So how could רב read ahead of a כהן?

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense (about this case), but… (introduces a contrast)
They were subordinate to him, they bowed to his authority
And he placed him above himself, showing him deference
Two leading כהנים and אמוראים in ארץ ישראל

phrases.english: Granted, Rav Huna would read in the priests' portion,

phrases.aramaic: דְּהָא אֲפִילּוּ רַב אַמֵּי וְרַב אַסִּי
phrases.english: for even Rav Ami and Rav Asi,
who were the esteemed priests of the Land of Israel,
were subordinate to Rav Huna.
But Rav? There was Shmuel,
who was a priest, and Rav placed him above himself!
phrases.notes: So רב was not the unrivaled leader.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the comparison of רב to רב הונא made in step 28.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רב read the כהנים' portion like רב הונא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Only an unrivaled leader may read before a כהן. רב deferred to שמואל, a כהן, so he did not fit that role.

steps.title: רב honored שמואל only when שמואל was present
steps.stepSummary: שמואל was actually subordinate to רב. רב honored him by choice, and only in his presence.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל too was subordinate to רב. It was רב who chose to show him honor. And when he did, it was only in שמואל's presence. When שמואל was not there, רב did not do it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. In truth רב was the greater one, and his honoring of שמואל was a personal choice that applied only when שמואל was present.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge assumed that שמואל ranked above רב. The answer flips this: by right, שמואל deferred to רב. רב gave שמואל honor voluntarily (some explain, to appease him), and only face to face. So when שמואל was absent, as on that fast day, רב was the leader and could read first.

keyTerms.meaning: Honor, respect
In his presence
Not in his presence

phrases.aramaic: שְׁמוּאֵל נָמֵי מִיכָּף הֲוָה כַּיִיף לֵיהּ לְרַב,
phrases.english: Shmuel too was subordinate to Rav,
and it was Rav who showed him honor,
phrases.notes: By his own choice.

phrases.english: and when he did so, it was in his presence;
not in his presence, he did not do so.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁמוּאֵל נָמֵי מִיכָּף הֲוָה כַּיִיף לֵיהּ לְרַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 29.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the facts: the honor was voluntary and limited to שמואל's presence.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב ranked below שמואל, so he could never read ahead of a כהן.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב was the senior leader. When שמואל was absent, רב could read first.

steps.title: Support that רב read first: he said the opening ברכה
steps.stepSummary: Logic supports that רב read first, because only the first reader says the opening ברכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: So too it is logical that רב read the כהנים' portion. For if you think he read the ישראל portion, why did he say the ברכה before reading?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support for the idea that רב read first. In step 26 we were told that רב said the opening ברכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under the original practice, only the first reader said a ברכה before reading. Since רב said the opening ברכה, it looks like he was the first reader, not the third. That would back up step 28.

keyTerms.meaning: So too it is logical (introduces support)
If it enters your mind (if you were to think)
Before it, meaning the ברכה before the reading

phrases.english: So too it is reasonable
that Rav read in the priests' portion,
for if you think he read in the Israelite's portion,
why did he bless before it?
phrases.notes: Only the first reader blessed beforehand.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי נָמֵי מִסְתַּבְּרָא דְּרַב בְּכָהֲנֵי קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings support for the claim of step 28 after it survived the challenge.
steps.raayaObject: That רב read the first portion.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב said the opening ברכה (step 26), which only the first reader said.

steps.title: No support: this happened after the תקנה that every reader blesses
steps.stepSummary: The support is rejected. By then, the rule had changed so that every reader says the opening ברכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: This was after the enactment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the support from step 31 in just two words. The story took place after the חכמים changed the rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Later, a תקנה was made that every person called up says a ברכה before reading. So רב's opening ברכה does not show that he was first. He could have been third and still blessed. The support falls, though step 28's suggestion still stands as a possibility.

keyTerms.meaning: An enactment of the חכמים
After

steps.confusionAlert: This rejects only the extra support from step 31. It does not knock down step 28's suggestion that רב read first. That suggestion is still possible, just not proven.

phrases.english: After the enactment.
phrases.notes: After the חכמים instituted that every reader blesses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the support of step 31.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the supporting argument from step 31.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The support assumed only the first reader blesses beforehand. After the תקנה, every reader does.

steps.title: Then He Should Have Said the Closing Blessing Too
steps.stepSummary: If the rule is that every reader says ברכות, רב should have said the closing ברכה after his reading as well.
steps.simpleTranslation: If that is so, he should also have said the blessing after it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from Step 32. If every reader now says ברכות, why did רב skip the ברכה after his reading?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 32 said the later rule was that every reader says the ברכה before reading. But that same rule also had every reader say the ברכה after reading. So the change in the rule explains the ברכה before, but it makes the missing ברכה after harder to explain.

keyTerms.meaning: If so; if that is true
After it (the blessing after the Torah reading)
He should say a blessing

phrases.english: If so,
phrases.notes: If every reader now says ברכות, as Step 32 said.

phrases.english: he should also have said the blessing after it!
phrases.notes: Under the new rule, each reader says a ברכה before and after.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the rejection in Step 32 by following its logic to the end.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 32 that every reader says ברכות under the later rule.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The later rule requires a ברכה both before and after. רב said only the first one. So the later rule does not fully explain what רב did.

steps.title: Where רב Was, People Kept Coming In
steps.stepSummary: The answer begins: it was different where רב was sitting, because people kept coming into the בית כנסת during the reading.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is different where רב was sitting, because people would come in.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts to answer the question from Step 33. It explains that where רב was, the situation was different. The answer is completed at the start of the next passage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule that every reader says ברכות was made for people who come late and people who leave early, so neither group would get the wrong idea about the ברכות. Where רב was, people did come in late, so the ברכה before was needed. The second half, that they did not leave early (so the ברכה after was not needed), comes on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: It is different
Where רב was sitting (present)
Because they would come in (people entering in the middle)

steps.confusionAlert: This is only half the answer. It explains why רב said the ברכה before. Why he skipped the ברכה after (no one left early) comes on the next amud.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the reason behind a rule (protecting latecomers and early leavers) decides how the rule is applied in a specific place.

phrases.english: It is different where Rav was sitting,
because people would come in,
phrases.notes: Latecomers kept arriving, so the ברכה before was needed for them. The next passage continues: but they did not leave.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts the answer to the question in Step 33.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the case: the reason for the rule applied only partly where רב was.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every reader must always say both ברכות, so רב's skipping the closing one makes no sense.
steps.terutzMaskana: Where רב was, people came in late but (as the next passage finishes) did not leave early. So only the ברכה before was needed.
